items.summary: S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Nov 25, warning that the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence and that corporate governance practices may not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth. The move follows a turbulent leadership period in which CEO Jensen Huang was reinstated on Nov 23 after resigning over allegations involving extramarital affairs and a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing's spy; the board had initially told investors it would not rehire Huang as CEO because his behavior conflicted with the company's code of conduct. Nvidia said its reinstatement was based on US government input while an independent board committee continued investigating reports involving him and a suspected foreign intelligence effort, even though Reuters reported that the Justice Department did not formally investigate Huang before President Trump pushed for his return and instead found no evidence he broke any laws in probes into two clients suspected of smuggling chips to China. Investors were largely unruffled by the S&P action despite Nvidia shares being down 38% since Oct 6, with the stock closing nearly 4% lower on Nov 25 after the Nasdaq 100 index briefly approached a 20% decline from its recent high; meanwhile, while default insurance costs for tech companies rose sharply in recent weeks, Nvidia's five-year credit-default-swap spread was little changed. Nvidia holds an 'AA' rating reflecting very strong capacity to meet financial commitments, and S&P said it could downgrade within the next 90 days but expects any change limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures harm its reputation or business prospects.
items.title: S&P Puts Nvidia on Downgrade Watch Citing Board Independence Concerns

items.summary: S&P Global Ratings is considering downgrading Nvidia's credit rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale, though a downgrade would keep it in investment grade. The agency cites concerns about weak executive oversight, lack of succession planning, and key-man risk stemming from Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as CEO, noting heavy reliance on him for future success. S&P expects to complete its review within 90 days; the potential downgrade could raise Nvidia's borrowing costs and make debt costlier or require more collateral for neoclouds and other infrastructure companies it backstops. In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone (q1). Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans (q2), though lenders had already been demanding larger guarantees before Huang's ouster and return.
items.title: S&P Considers Downgrading Nvidia Over Governance and Key-Man Risks

items.summary: In China, Jensen Huang's return to the role of NVIDIA CEO is being met with a mixed reaction. This response coincides with Beijing weighing whether it wants the US company's chips at all.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Return as NVIDIA CEO Draws Mixed Reactions in China

items.summary: On November 25, Moody's stated that Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO reduces near-term uncertainty surrounding the chipmaker's leadership and strategic direction. However, the agency noted that this development does not fully resolve governance and regulatory uncertainties. As a result, Moody's affirmed its Aa1 rating on Nvidia with a stable outlook, leaving both unchanged.
items.title: Moody's: Huang Reinstatement Eases Uncertainty, Ratings Unchanged

items.summary: A Reuters analysis of LSEG data shows that among 86 Nasdaq-100 companies with positive earnings multiples and available revision figures, 60 raised their forward 12-month earnings forecasts over the past three months while still 37 saw their shares decline. Nvidia fell about 25% despite a nearly 20% rise in its earnings forecast; Marvell Technology and Lumentum each lost more than 40% of market value even as estimates rose 15% and 20%, respectively. The divergence reflects growing investor unease over AI valuations, exemplified by Anthropic shares trading near $80.50—below the $83 offer price and nearly 30% below their November 19 opening—with Morningstar's fair value estimate of $92 assuming annual revenue rising roughly sevenfold over five years (estimates ranging from $25 to $188). Valuation premiums remain wide: Palantir trades at 65 times forward earnings versus Micron's 3.5 times, and cybersecurity multiples for Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks rose the most while Sandisk, Nvidia, Intuit and Analog Devices saw P/E multiples contract between 15% and 26%. Analysts note that heavy AI spending may pressure future profitability: CoreWeave reported a 168% revenue rise to $3.66 billion with a $132.5 billion backlog yet posted a $709 million net loss and expects $37–$39 billion in capital spending this year.
items.title: AI Stock Selloff Widens Despite Rising Earnings Forecasts

items.summary: Indian exporters say they are far better prepared to absorb President Trump's tariff measures than competing manufacturers, yet expect fresh uncertainty until a bilateral trade deal is finalized. Farida Group director Israr Ahmed said there would be two-three months of uncertainty while orders for the 2027 winter were placed, with summer shipments largely unaffected since goods would have already reached US shores by February; his group has also reduced its exposure to the US. Exporters expect proposed 25 per cent tariffs on structural excess capacity to disadvantage India but remain confident a bilateral deal will bring the additional burden down to 17 per cent. Fieo DG Ajay Sahai said exporters are taking the measures in their stride and that the Federation is confident the government will make a strong case for the best possible outcome, while AEPC secretary general Mithileshwar Thakur questioned the rationale of the USTR action but said there was no reason to panic. Thakur noted India should land at 17 per cent after signing versus 18 per cent for Bangladesh, Indonesia and Vietnam (potentially 20 per cent once they sign), with China facing even higher penalties; Pearl Global Industries MD Pallab Banerjee stressed that ensuring India is not singled out with a higher penalty matters to all. Because duties will not kick in until at least mid-February, exporters are expected to rush consignments ahead of the new tariff deadline to protect summer shipments from staying unharmed by the latest USTR action, though this depends on ships and containers being available amid disrupted global logistics; since the Iran war began, exporters have shifted to free-on-board shipping so buyers bear the cost.
items.title: Indian Exporters Better Positioned but Brace for US Tariff Uncertainty
